title: The Paper Revolution in China
summary: Long ago in China, people wrote on heavy bamboo sticks and costly silk. Then clever workers learned to turn mushy plant fibers and old rags into thin, light sheets: paper! It was cheap, it was smooth, and it soon spread to Korea and Japan.

sections.heading: Books You Needed a Cart to Carry
paragraphs: Imagine you are a government clerk in China about 2,100 years ago. Your desk is not covered in sheets of paper. Instead it is stacked with bundles of thin bamboo strips, each one about as long as a ruler and as wide as a finger. You write on them with a brush dipped in black ink, one narrow column of characters per strip, from top to bottom. When a document is finished, the strips are tied together with cords, like a little bamboo fence, and then rolled up into a bundle.

These strips are called jiandu, which means something like 'slips and tablets'. Bamboo grew in huge forests across central and southern China, so it was easy to find. Workers cut the stems into strips, scraped them smooth and dried them over a gentle fire so they would not rot or crack or get eaten by insects. In the dry northwest, where bamboo did not grow, people used thin slips of wood instead. Archaeologists have dug up tens of thousands of these slips from tombs and old army outposts, many of them still readable.

Bamboo worked, but it had one enormous problem: weight. A single long book could fill dozens of bundles. An old Chinese history says that the First Emperor of Qin, who unified China in 221 BCE, set himself a goal of reading a fixed weight of documents every day before he rested, measured on a scale. Whether or not that story is exactly true, it tells us something real: Chinese rulers measured their paperwork in kilograms, because it really was heavy. Moving a library meant loading carts.

Bamboo books had other troubles too. The cords that held the strips together could rot or snap, and then the strips fell out of order. Scholars today spend years puzzling over ancient bamboo texts whose strips got jumbled in the ground, like a jigsaw puzzle with no picture on the box.

There was a lighter choice: silk. Chinese weavers had been making silk for thousands of years, and a piece of silk cloth could be written on, folded, and carried easily. In 1973 archaeologists opening a tomb at Mawangdui, in today's Hunan province, found silk sheets covered with writing and even maps, buried in 168 BCE. But silk was precious. It was one of the most valuable goods in the ancient world, traded all the way to Rome. Writing a long letter on silk was a bit like writing your homework on a fancy silk scarf. Only the rich could afford it often.

So China had two writing surfaces: one cheap but heavy, one light but expensive. What people really needed was something in between, as light as silk and as cheap as bamboo. That something turned out to be paper.

sections.heading: Paper Before the Famous Inventor
paragraphs: For a long time, schoolbooks said paper was invented in the year 105 CE by a man named Cai Lun. That date still matters, and we will meet Cai Lun soon. But the ground in China has been telling a different, more interesting story.

In 1986, archaeologists were excavating a group of tombs at a place called Fangmatan, near the city of Tianshui in Gansu province, in northwest China. In Tomb 5, which dates to the early part of the Western Han dynasty, around the 2nd century BCE, they found something remarkable. The man buried there had a map laid on his chest, and the map was drawn on paper. Water had seeped into the tomb over the centuries, so only a small scrap survived, only a few centimeters across, roughly the size of a domino. But on that scrap you can still see thin black lines showing mountains, rivers and roads.

That little scrap is often described as one of the oldest surviving pieces of paper in the world, and it is roughly 250 to 300 years older than Cai Lun's famous report. Historians date it to roughly 179 to 141 BCE.

Fangmatan is not alone. Other finds of early Han paper have turned up in different parts of China. At a site called Xuanquan, a Han dynasty relay station on the road near Dunhuang where messengers changed horses, archaeologists in the 1990s found many fragments of paper, a few of them with writing on them. Another find, from near the old capital city of Xi'an in 1957, is called Baqiao paper. Experts still argue about whether the Baqiao fragments are true paper or just a matted clump of fibers, which shows how careful scientists have to be.

Many of these early papers seem to have been rough and thick. Some were probably used for wrapping things, like medicines or bronze mirrors, rather than for writing. That makes sense: when a new material first appears, people often use it for simple jobs before they discover its best uses.

So paper was not invented in a single flash by one person. It grew slowly, probably over generations, in workshops where people noticed that fibers soaked in water could be laid out to make a thin, flexible mat. That is how many inventions really happen: lots of nameless people improving an idea a little at a time, until someone makes it good enough, and famous enough, to change the world.

sections.heading: Cai Lun and His Report to the Emperor
paragraphs: Now let us meet the man whose name is forever tied to paper. Cai Lun was born around the middle of the 1st century CE in Guiyang, a district in what is now Hunan province in southern China. As a young man he went to serve in the palace of the Eastern Han dynasty in the capital, Luoyang. He became a trusted court official and rose to an important job: he was put in charge of the imperial workshops, where skilled craftsmen made weapons, tools and fine objects for the emperor's household. Cai Lun was known for being careful and hardworking, and for paying close attention to how things were made.

In the year 105 CE, according to the official history of the Han dynasty, Cai Lun presented a report to Emperor He about a better way to make paper. The history explains the problem he was solving: bamboo was heavy and silk was expensive, and neither was convenient. Cai Lun's idea was to make paper from cheap things that were easy to find: the inner bark of trees, scraps of hemp, old rags of cloth, and worn-out fishing nets.

Think about how clever that list is. Rags and old fishing nets were trash. Hemp waste was left over after making rope and cloth. Tree bark grew everywhere. By using leftovers, Cai Lun turned rubbish into a valuable product. In a way, it was one of history's earliest recycling ideas.

The emperor was pleased. The history says that from then on, paper came into use everywhere, and people called it 'the paper of Marquis Cai', because Cai Lun was later given the noble title of marquis. Whether paper truly spread 'everywhere' right away is doubtful, since bamboo slips stayed in use for another couple of centuries. But Cai Lun's method, backed by the emperor, gave papermaking an official stamp of approval, better recipes, and a big push.

Cai Lun's own story did not end happily. Palace life in Han China was full of rivalries between powerful families. Years earlier, Cai Lun had been involved in a dispute that harmed the grandmother of the later Emperor An. When Emperor An took full power in 121 CE, he ordered Cai Lun to report to the authorities for punishment. Rather than face disgrace, Cai Lun dressed in his finest robes and ended his own life by taking poison. It is a sad ending for a man who gave the world such a useful gift.

Over the following centuries, Cai Lun was honored more and more. Papermakers in China came to treat him as the patron, or special protector, of their craft, and shrines and temples were built in his memory. In his hometown area, a memorial park still stands today. In 2008, during the opening ceremony of the Beijing Olympic Games, paper was celebrated in front of a worldwide audience as one of ancient China's great inventions.

Remember the fair way to say it: Cai Lun did not invent paper from nothing. Older paper already existed. What he did was improve the method, use better and cheaper materials, and present it to the emperor so it became widely known. That is still a huge achievement. And the official history that tells his story, the Book of the Later Han, was written in the 400s CE, more than 300 years after he lived, so historians read its details with some caution.

sections.heading: How to Make Paper: The Science of Soggy Fibers
paragraphs: Paper looks simple, but it is a small miracle of science. Let us follow the steps a papermaker in Han China might have used, and see what is happening at each stage.

Step one: gather fibers. Plants are built from tiny tubes and threads made of a material called cellulose. Cellulose is what makes celery stringy and wood strong. The best papermaking plants have long, tough cellulose fibers. In China, favorites were the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree, hemp, ramie (a kind of nettle) and later bamboo. Old rags and fishing nets were useful because they were already made of hemp or similar fibers.

Step two: soak and cook. The fibers were soaked in water and often boiled with wood ash or lime. Ash mixed with water makes an alkaline liquid that softens the plant material and loosens the gummy substances that hold fibers together in the plant. After cooking, the stuff would be soft and floppy.

Step three: beat it. Workers pounded the softened fibers with wooden mallets or stones, or with foot-powered hammers. Beating does two jobs. It separates the fibers from one another, and it frays their surfaces, so each fiber becomes fuzzy with tiny side threads, called fibrils. Those fuzzy edges are important, as we will see.
Step four: make the pulp. The beaten fibers were stirred into a big vat of water, making a thin, milky soup called pulp. Most of the soup is water; only a small part is fiber.

Step five: form the sheet. Here comes the clever part. The papermaker takes a mould, which is a frame with a screen stretched across it, a little like a sieve. Early Chinese papermakers sometimes used a frame covered with woven cloth, floated on the water, and poured pulp onto it. Later, they used screens made of very thin strips of bamboo that could be dipped straight into the vat and lifted out. As the screen rises, the water drains through the tiny gaps, but the fibers are caught on top, forming a thin, even layer, like a wet spiderweb of fibers crossing in every direction.
Step six: press and dry. The wet sheet is turned out onto a flat surface, pressed to squeeze out more water, and then dried, often by brushing it onto a warm wall or a board in the sun.

Now the big question: when the sheet dries, why does it hold together, with no glue at all? The answer lies in the cellulose molecules. Cellulose is covered with tiny groups of atoms that include oxygen and hydrogen. When the fibers are wet, water molecules sit between them. As the water evaporates, the shrinking film of water pulls the fibers closer and closer together, until their surfaces are almost touching. Then weak attractions between the molecules on neighboring fibers, such as hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, snap into place where the fibers cross. Each bond is incredibly weak, but there are trillions of them, and together they lock the whole tangled web into a strong, flexible sheet.

This also explains a fact you can test at home: wet paper tears easily. When you soak paper, water molecules slip back in between the fibers and break apart many of those tiny bonds. The fibers can then slide apart. When it dries again, many bonds re-form, but the sheet is usually wrinkly and weaker. The fuzzy, frayed fibrils made by beating matter because they create far more contact points between fibers, so the paper ends up stronger.

sections.heading: A Visit to a Papermakers' Workshop
paragraphs: No one filmed a Han dynasty paper workshop, of course, but we can piece together a good picture from old tools, surviving paper and later Chinese books that describe the craft. Let us imagine stepping inside one on a cool spring morning, somewhere beside a river in central China.

The first thing you notice is the water. Papermaking needs a lot of clean water, which is why workshops were built beside streams and rivers. Bundles of bark sit soaking in a pool, slowly softening. Nearby, a big pot of ash and water bubbles over a fire, and a worker stirs the steaming mass of fibers with a long pole. The air smells of wet wood and smoke.

In one corner, two workers take turns pounding a heap of cooked fibers on a flat stone. Thud, thud, thud. Hour after hour they beat, until the stringy mass becomes a soft, fluffy paste. It is hard, tiring work. Much later, Chinese papermakers used heavy hammers lifted by a foot-pedal or even by a waterwheel, which made beating much faster.

At the center of the room stands the vat, a big wooden or stone tub full of cloudy water. The most skilled worker in the workshop stands here. He dips his screen into the vat at a slight angle, scoops up pulp, lifts the screen level and gives it a gentle shake so the fibers spread evenly. Water rains back into the vat. In just a few seconds, a pale wet sheet has formed on the screen. Making every sheet the same thickness takes years of practice; a beginner's sheets come out lumpy, too thick in some places and full of holes in others.

The sheet is flipped onto a growing stack. When the stack is tall enough, it is pressed under heavy weights to squeeze out water. Then, one by one, the damp sheets are peeled off and brushed onto a smooth heated wall to dry. A few minutes later they can be peeled off, dry, flat and ready to use.

A good team could make hundreds of sheets in a day. Compare that with the time it took to cut, scrape, dry and bind bamboo slips, or to raise silkworms, spin their thread and weave silk cloth, and you can see why paper won.

Centuries later, in 1637, a Chinese scholar named Song Yingxing published an illustrated encyclopedia of crafts and technology called the Tiangong Kaiwu, often translated as 'The Exploitation of the Works of Nature'. Its woodcut pictures show every step of making paper from bamboo: soaking stalks in a pit, cooking them, pounding them, dipping the screen in the vat, pressing the stack and drying sheets on a heated wall. These pictures are some of the best views we have of traditional Chinese papermaking, and the basic steps they show had been worked out many centuries earlier.

sections.heading: Why Paper Was Such a Big Deal
paragraphs: Put a bundle of bamboo slips next to a stack of paper holding the same words, and the difference is shocking. The paper might weigh only a small fraction as much and take up far less space. Suddenly a scholar could carry a small library in a box instead of a cart.

Paper was also cheap, especially once workshops used rags, hemp scraps and fast-growing plants. It was smooth, so the soft tip of a writing brush glided across it. And it soaked up ink in just the right way. Chinese ink was made from soot mixed with animal glue and pressed into solid sticks; the writer ground the stick with a little water on a stone to make liquid ink. On good paper, this ink sank into the fibers and stayed sharp and black for centuries.

Paper could be cut to any size, folded, rolled into scrolls, pasted together into long sheets, or stacked. You could write big or small. Painters soon discovered it, and Chinese painting and calligraphy, the art of beautiful writing, grew up alongside paper.

Papermakers kept improving their product. They learned to coat paper with a thin layer of starch or other materials so that ink would not spread and blur; this coating is called sizing. They also dyed paper with a yellow liquid made from the bark of the Amur cork tree, called huangbo. The dye gave paper a golden color and helped keep away insects that liked to eat paper. Many old Buddhist scrolls from the Dunhuang caves are this golden-yellow color.

Change still took time. For two centuries or so after Cai Lun, Chinese officials used both bamboo and paper. By around the 300s CE, paper had become the normal material for writing, and bamboo slips were fading away. A famous step came around 404 CE, when a powerful warlord named Huan Xuan is said to have ordered his officials to use paper instead of bamboo slips for official documents. Some historians see this as the moment paper finally won.

Paper also found jobs nobody had imagined. During the Tang dynasty (618 to 907 CE), Chinese people made paper cups, paper napkins and folded paper bags for storing tea. Paper was used for windows, letting soft light into rooms while blocking wind, and for fans, kites, lanterns and umbrellas. Much later, in the Song dynasty, China printed the world's first government paper money. Few inventions have ever had so many uses.

Most important of all, paper made writing affordable for many more people. Students could practice their characters, merchants could keep records, and poets could jot down verses. More writing surface meant more writing, and more writing meant more copying, more letters and more books. That huge pile of words would one day create a demand for a faster way to copy them: printing.

sections.heading: Paper Crosses to Korea and Japan
paragraphs: China's neighbors soon wanted this marvelous material. Ideas and goods moved back and forth between China and the Korean peninsula for centuries, carried by merchants, officials, monks and soldiers. During the Han dynasty, China even governed parts of northern Korea for a time. Historians think papermaking knowledge probably reached Korea somewhere between the 3rd and 6th centuries CE, although no one knows the exact date.

Buddhism played a big part. This religion began in India and spread through Central Asia to China and then to Korea and Japan. Buddhist monks wanted to copy holy texts called sutras, and copying a sutra was considered a good and holy deed. That created an enormous demand for paper and ink. Korean papermakers became famous for their own paper, now called hanji, made from the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree. Hanji is known for being strong and long-lasting, and it is still made by hand in Korea today.

Japan's story has a well-known starting point. An ancient Japanese history called the Nihon Shoki, finished in 720 CE, says that in the year 610 a Buddhist monk named Damjing (called Donchō in Japanese) arrived from the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo. The history says he knew how to make paints, paper and ink, and also built a water-powered mill. For centuries this has been told as the moment papermaking arrived in Japan. But historians point out that the text does not clearly say he introduced papermaking for the first time, and Japan may already have had paper before 610. So it is best to call 610 the traditional date.

Either way, Japanese papermakers made the craft their own. Japanese paper is called washi, and it is often made from kozo, the Japanese name for paper mulberry bark, as well as other plants called mitsumata and gampi. Japanese makers developed a technique of rocking the mould back and forth in the vat so that long fibers crossed in many layers, making paper that is thin yet surprisingly tough. Some very old Japanese documents on paper still survive, kept for over 1,200 years in a treasure house at Nara called the Shōsōin. In 2014 UNESCO added traditional Japanese washi papermaking to its list of the world's Intangible Cultural Heritage.

By around the 600s CE, then, paper was being made across East Asia: in China, in Korea and in Japan. Each region used local plants and invented its own tools and styles, but they all shared the same basic recipe that Chinese workers had pioneered centuries earlier: beat fibers, mix them with water, catch them on a screen and let them dry.

In these same lands, in these same centuries, people were also carving seals and stamping charms and pictures, getting closer and closer to the idea of printing whole pages. That is a story for a later part of this Deep Dive. For now, keep in mind that without cheap paper, printing would never have caught on. You cannot print a million copies on silk, and you certainly cannot press a printing block against a bundle of bamboo strips.
Paper was ready. Over the next few centuries, it would begin its long journey west.

deepDive: Two debates sit underneath this chapter. The first is about credit. The traditional date of 105 CE comes from the biography of Cai Lun in the Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), compiled by Fan Ye in the 400s CE, more than three centuries after the events. For a long time it was read as the moment paper was invented. Archaeology changed that. The Fangmatan map fragment (Tomb 5, excavated 1986) is generally dated to the early Western Han, around the 2nd century BCE, and Han-era paper has also been found at sites such as Xuanquan near Dunhuang. The Baqiao find from near Xi'an (1957) is more controversial: some specialists argue it is a loose mat of fibers rather than a sheet formed on a screen, which raises a useful question of definition. Most historians therefore describe Cai Lun as an improver and promoter, perhaps a standardizer of good recipes in the imperial workshops, rather than the first inventor. That is not a demotion: making a technology cheap, reliable and officially approved is often what actually changes the world. The second debate is about chemistry. Textbooks usually say paper holds together because hydrogen bonds form between the hydroxyl (OH) groups on neighboring cellulose fibers as the sheet dries, and capillary forces during drying pull the fibers into close contact. That explanation is a good first answer, and it neatly explains why wet paper loses most of its strength. But researchers still argue about the details. In a 2015 study in Scientific Reports, Ulrich Hirn and Robert Schennach of Graz University of Technology estimated the contributions of several mechanisms: hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, electrostatic (Coulomb) attraction, capillary bridges, mechanical interlocking of fibrils, and interdiffusion of molecules. Their model suggested that van der Waals forces may contribute more than hydrogen bonds, while all the mechanisms depend heavily on how much area of the fibers comes into true molecular contact. That is why beating, which frays fibers and increases contact area, matters so much for strength. The safe summary: many weak molecular attractions, including van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds, glue a paper sheet together without any added adhesive.
funFact: One of the oldest known pieces of paper in the world, from a tomb at Fangmatan in China, is a scrap of a map only a few centimeters across, roughly the size of a domino.

check.q: What cheap materials did Cai Lun suggest for making paper in 105 CE?
check.a: Tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets
